direct_answer: Stairs are a common challenge with knee osteoarthritis and frailty. Going up with the stronger leg first and down with the painful leg first, using banisters on both sides, good lighting and strength exercises can help. An occupational therapist can assess your stairs.
author: Louis Maxwell

content:
Stairs need strength, balance and confidence, all of which knee pain and frailty can affect.

This guide covers safer ways to manage stairs. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Technique

  • Up with the stronger leg first.
  • Down with the painful leg first.
  • One step at a time.
  • Hold the banister.

Make stairs safer

  • A second banister.
  • Good lighting, including two-way switches.
  • Contrasting step edges.
  • Keep stairs clear.

Strength

Strength exercises such as sit-to-stand and step-ups, if advised, can help.

Assessment

Ask your council for an occupational therapy assessment. Options range from rails to a stairlift or living downstairs.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Should I avoid stairs?

Not necessarily; they can help keep you strong if safe.

Can I get a second rail free?

Minor adaptations are often free after assessment.
